expected score.def: The average points per question you would get if you faced the same situation many times. For a Part 1 answer that is right with probability p, it is 7.5p.

try block.def: A box of code in a lesson that you can edit and run. The last line's value is shown, as in a notebook cell.

google colab.def: A website that runs Python notebooks on a Google computer. Part 2 of Round 1 is solved in it.

notebook.def: A document made of code cells and text cells, saved as an .ipynb file.

cell.def: One box in a notebook: either a code cell (Python, runs and shows output) or a text cell (Markdown and math).

runtime.def: The Python process on a Google machine that runs a notebook's cells. Variables, imports and functions live in its memory, not in the notebook file.

hidden state.def: Variables left in the runtime's memory by cells run earlier, run out of order, or since deleted. It makes a notebook work on your screen but fail when run fresh.

markdown.def: A plain-text way to format writing: # for headings, **bold**, - for bullet lists, backticks for code. Colab text cells use it.

latex.def: The standard way to type math as text, for example \frac{a}{b} for a fraction. In a text cell it goes between $ signs (inline) or $$ signs (display).

module.def: A .py file that other code can import. Importing runs the file once and gives access to its functions and classes as attributes, like sub.f.

%%writefile.def: A Colab (Jupyter) command that, as the first line of a cell, saves the rest of the cell into a file instead of running it.

grader.def: The program that scores a Part 2 submission: it imports your file, calls your function or class on hidden inputs, and checks results, imports, banned names, time and input mutation.

open-ended problem.def: A Part 2 problem where you choose and train any model you like, and it is scored on a hidden test set.

checkpoint.def: A saved file holding a model's learned numbers (and usually the settings needed to rebuild it), so another notebook can load the trained model without retraining.

proctor.def: The approved adult at your test site who supervises the contest, gives the site code, and is the only one who can remove a temporary lock.

type.def: The kind of a value, such as int, float, bool, str, list or None. type(x) shows it.

floor division.def: The // operator: divide, then round down toward minus infinity. -7 // 2 is -4.

truncation.def: Dropping the fractional part of a number, moving toward zero. int(-2.7) is -2.

round half to even.def: Python's rule for round(): a value exactly halfway between two integers goes to the even one. round(2.5) is 2, round(3.5) is 4.

tolerance.def: The largest difference still counted as equal when comparing floats, as in abs(a - b) <= 1e-9.

truthiness.def: Whether a value counts as true in an if: zero (0, 0.0), None, False and empty strings or containers are falsy; every nonzero number (negative too) and every nonempty string or container is truthy. So if x % 2 keeps odd x.

tuple.def: An ordered sequence that cannot be changed after it is made, written (3, 4). Functions return several values as a tuple.

unpacking.def: Assigning the items of a sequence to several names at once: a, b = (1, 2).

dict.def: A mapping from keys to values, written {"cat": 0}. Looking up a missing key with d[key] raises KeyError.

set.def: An unordered collection of distinct values, written {1, 2}. len(set(xs)) counts distinct values.

comprehension.def: A one-expression way to build a list, dict or set: [f(x) for x in xs if condition].

function parameter.def: A name in a function's def line that receives a value when the function is called.

argument.def: A value passed to a function in a call.

keyword argument.def: An argument passed by parameter name, as in f(x, shift=5).

default value.def: A value a parameter takes when the call leaves it out, as in def f(x, factor=2).

keyword-only parameter.def: A parameter after a lone * in the def line; it can only be passed by name.

lambda.def: A one-expression function written inline, as in lambda x: x * x. Common as the key= of sorted, min and max.

stable sort.def: A sort that keeps equal elements in their original order. Python's sorted and .sort are stable.

class (python).def: A blueprint for a kind of object, defining its attributes and methods.

instance.def: An object made from a class. Counter(5) makes a new instance of Counter.

method.def: A function defined inside a class. Called as obj.method(args); Python passes the object as self.

constructor.def: The __init__ method. It runs automatically when you create an object, to set up its attributes.

self.def: The first parameter of every method: the object the method is working on. Python fills it in automatically.

attribute.def: A variable stored on an object, set and read as self.name or obj.name.

learned parameters.def: The numbers a model computes from training data in fit, such as weights or a mean.

inheritance.def: Building a new class from an existing one: class Child(Parent) gets all of Parent's methods.

subclass.def: A class that inherits from another: in class Child(Parent), Child is a subclass of Parent.

parent class.def: The class a subclass inherits from (also called the base class).

override.def: To define, in a subclass, a method with the same name as the parent's, so the subclass's version is used.

super().def: Gives access to the parent class's version of a method from inside a subclass, as in super().__init__().

package.def: A folder of modules that can be imported, such as torch; torch.nn is a submodule inside it.

alias.def: A second name for the same thing: import numpy as np makes np an alias for numpy, and b = a makes b another name for a's object.

json.def: A text format for nested data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true/false/null). Its object keys are always strings.

csv.def: A table stored as text: one row per line, values separated by commas, usually with a header row.

exception.def: An error object Python raises when something goes wrong, with a type (such as KeyError) and a message.

traceback.def: The report Python prints for an uncaught exception: the chain of calls, oldest first, then the exception type and message on the last line.

mutate.def: To change an object in place, so every name pointing at it sees the change.

mutable.def: Able to be changed in place: lists, dicts, sets, NumPy arrays, DataFrames and tensors.

immutable.def: Unable to be changed in place: ints, floats, bools, strings, tuples and None.

shallow copy.def: A new outer container holding the same inner objects, made by list(a), a[:], a.copy() or dict(d).

deep copy.def: A copy of an object and everything inside it, made by copy.deepcopy.

closure.def: A function that uses names from the place where it was created (a loop, a comprehension or an enclosing function). It looks those names up when it runs.

late binding.def: Looking up a name's value when a function runs rather than when it is created. Lambdas made in a loop all see the loop variable's final value; a default such as i=i freezes the current one.

generator.def: A function containing yield, or an expression like (x * x for x in xs). Calling it runs nothing; each next() runs the body to the next yield. It can be read only once.

iterator.def: An object that hands out values one at a time through next() and is used up after one pass. Generators and the results of zip, map, filter and enumerate are iterators.

method resolution order.def: MRO: the order of classes Python searches for a method, shown by Cls.__mro__. super() calls the next class in the MRO of the object's own class, which is not always the parent.

array.def: A NumPy grid of numbers (an ndarray) in which every entry has the same type. Arithmetic on an array acts on every entry.

shape.def: The tuple of an array's lengths along each axis, e.g. (2, 3) for 2 rows and 3 columns. Read it with a.shape.

axis.def: One direction of an array, numbered from 0. For shape (n, d), axis 0 runs down the rows and axis 1 across the columns.

sample.def: One example in a dataset (one patient, one image). In a data table X of shape (n, d), each row is a sample.

feature.def: One measured quantity describing each sample (age, pixel brightness). In a data table X of shape (n, d), each column is a feature.

dtype.def: The data type shared by all entries of an array, such as int64, float64 or bool. Assigning a float into an int array cuts off the fraction.

row-major order.def: The order NumPy reads and fills entries in reshape: row by row, with the last axis changing fastest.

view.def: An array that shares memory with another array, made by basic slicing, reshape, ravel or .T. Writing into a view changes the original.

slice.def: An index of the form start:stop:step. The stop is excluded, and a slice keeps its axis even when it has length 1.

in-place.def: An operation that overwrites an existing array instead of making a new one, such as x -= m or x[mask] = 0. On a function's input it changes the caller's data.

elementwise.def: Done entry by entry: for arrays of the same shape, a + b adds matching entries.

ufunc.def: Universal function: a NumPy function such as np.exp, np.log or np.maximum that acts on every entry of an array.

nan.def: Not a number: the float value for an undefined result such as sqrt(-1) or 0/0. Any arithmetic with nan gives nan; test for it with np.isnan.

relu.def: The function max(0, x) applied to every entry. Neural networks use it between layers.

sigmoid.def: The function 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), which squashes any real number into (0, 1). Logistic regression uses it to turn a score into a probability.

reduction.def: An operation that turns many numbers into fewer, such as sum, mean, max or argmax, either over the whole array or along an axis.

keepdims.def: The reduction argument keepdims=True, which keeps the reduced axis with length 1 (shape (n, 1) instead of (n,)) so the result broadcasts back against the original.

mean.def: The average (1/n) times the sum of the values.

variance.def: The mean squared distance from the mean, (1/n) times the sum of (x_i - mean)^2. This is the population variance.

standard deviation.def: The square root of the variance. It measures spread in the data's own units.

sample variance.def: The variance computed with n - 1 in the denominator instead of n (np.var(x, ddof=1)).

class (classification).def: In classification, one of the k categories a sample can belong to, numbered 0 to k-1.

label.def: The true class of a sample (or the true value it should match), stored as an integer 0 to k-1 for classification.

classifier.def: A model that predicts a sample's class, usually by giving one score per class and picking the highest.

broadcasting.def: NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes: line the shapes up from the right; each pair of lengths must be equal or contain a 1, and length-1 axes are stretched to match.

outer product.def: For vectors u and v, the matrix u v^T whose entry (i, j) is u_i v_j. In NumPy: u[:, None] * v[None, :].

regression.def: Predicting a number (rather than a class) for each sample.

target.def: The true value a model's prediction should match for one sample.

boolean mask.def: An array of True and False used as an index: x[mask] keeps the entries where the mask is True, and x[mask] = v assigns only there.

fancy indexing.def: Indexing with an array of integers. It picks those positions in order, repeats allowed, and returns a copy. X[rows, cols] pairs the two index arrays entry by entry.

accuracy.def: The fraction of predictions that equal the true labels: (pred == y).mean().

cross-entropy loss.def: The usual loss for classifiers: the mean over samples of -log of the probability the model gave to the true class.

one-hot encoding.def: Turning an integer label c out of k classes into a length-k vector with 1 at position c and 0 elsewhere.

transpose.def: The matrix with rows and columns swapped: entry [i, j] moves to [j, i]. In NumPy A.T or np.transpose(A); it does nothing to a 1D array.

batched matmul.def: Many matrix products at once: (B, n, k) @ (B, k, m) gives (B, n, m), one product per leading index.

einsum.def: np.einsum writes a product by naming each axis with a letter; letters missing after -> are summed over, e.g. 'ij,jk->ik' is the matrix product.

loss.def: A number that measures how wrong a model's predictions are. Training changes the parameters to make it small.

mean squared error.def: The loss (1/N) times the sum over samples of (prediction - target)^2.

residual.def: The difference between a target and the model's prediction for one sample, such as r_n = y_n - theta^T x_n.

parameters.def: A model's adjustable numbers, such as weights and biases. Training changes them to make the loss small.

vectorize.def: To replace a Python loop over entries with whole-array NumPy operations, which run far faster.

euclidean distance.def: Straight-line distance: the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences, ||a - b||.

logits.def: The raw real-valued scores a classifier outputs, one per class, before softmax turns them into probabilities.

softmax.def: The map from scores z to probabilities e^(z_i) / sum_j e^(z_j). Subtracting max(z) first gives the same result without overflow.

overflow.def: A float result too large to store, which becomes inf (np.exp(1000.0) is inf).

underflow.def: A positive float result too small to store, which becomes exactly 0 (np.exp(-2000.0) is 0.0).

numerically stable.def: Computed in a way that gives correct answers despite float limits such as overflow, underflow and rounding.

log-sum-exp.def: LSE(z) = log of the sum of e^(z_j), computed stably as m + log sum e^(z_j - m) with m = max(z). Log-softmax is z - LSE(z).

pseudo-random number generator.def: A fixed algorithm whose output looks random. The same seed always produces the same sequence.

seed.def: The integer that sets a random number generator's starting point, e.g. np.random.default_rng(2026). Same seed, same numbers.

normal distribution.def: The bell-curve distribution with a mean and a standard deviation; values cluster around the mean.

permutation.def: The numbers 0, 1, ..., n-1 in some order. rng.permutation(n) returns a random one.

training set.def: The part of the data a model learns from.

test set.def: Held-out data the model never saw during training, used only to measure how well it does.

k-nearest neighbors.def: kNN: a classifier that predicts the most common label among the k training points closest to the query point.

moving average.def: The sequence of means of every run of w consecutive values; computed fast from cumulative sums.

k-means.def: A clustering algorithm: from k starting centers, repeatedly assign each point to its nearest center, then move each center to the mean of its points.

strides.def: For each axis of an array, the number of bytes to move in memory to reach the next entry along that axis. Slicing and transposing change only the shape and strides, which is why they make views.

contiguous array.def: An array whose entries sit in memory in row-major order with no gaps. reshape of a contiguous array is a view; reshape of a transposed or strided slice usually has to copy.

shape rule.def: A product AB needs columns of A = rows of B; then (m x n)(n x p) = (m x p).

dot product.def: x . y = sum of x_i y_i, also written x^T y; one number. A linear model's prediction is a dot product plus a bias.

norm.def: A length of a vector. With no subscript it means the L2 norm.

l2 norm.def: ||x||_2 = square root of the sum of x_i^2, the ordinary Euclidean length.

unit vector.def: A vector of norm 1; v / ||v|| is the unit vector in the direction of v.

cosine similarity.def: x . y / (||x|| ||y||), the cosine of the angle between x and y: 1 same direction, 0 orthogonal, -1 opposite.

cauchy-schwarz inequality.def: |x . y| <= ||x|| ||y||, which keeps cosine similarity between -1 and 1.

linear map.def: A map with f(ax + by) = a f(x) + b f(y); every one is multiplication by a matrix.

standard basis.def: The vectors e_j with a 1 in position j and 0 elsewhere. Column j of a matrix is the image of e_j.

linear layer.def: A neural network layer computing y = W x + b, with W of shape (outputs, inputs).

identity matrix.def: I: the square matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; I x = x, the matrix of the do-nothing map.

span.def: The set of all linear combinations of some vectors.

linear independence.def: No vector in the set is a linear combination of the others.

basis.def: An independent set of vectors that spans a subspace; its size is the dimension.

column space.def: All outputs Ax of a matrix A: the span of its columns.

rank.def: The dimension of the column space: the number of independent columns (equal to the number of independent rows).

rank-nullity theorem.def: rank(A) + dim null(A) = number of columns of A.

invertible matrix.def: A square matrix A with an inverse A^{-1} (A^{-1} A = I); equivalently full rank, or det A != 0.

singular matrix.def: A square matrix that is not invertible (determinant 0).

determinant.def: The factor by which a square matrix scales volume (signed); 0 exactly when the matrix is not invertible.

projection.def: The closest point to x in a line or subspace; for a unit vector e it is (x . e) e.

scalar projection.def: x . e for a unit vector e: the signed length of x along e.

projection residual.def: x minus its projection; it is orthogonal to the line or subspace projected onto.

normal equations.def: A^T A c = A^T x: the condition that the residual x - Ac is orthogonal to every column of A.

projection matrix.def: P = A (A^T A)^{-1} A^T, which projects onto the column space of A; symmetric with P^2 = P.

orthonormal.def: Unit length and mutually orthogonal. A matrix Q with orthonormal columns has Q^T Q = I.

least squares.def: Choosing w to minimize ||Xw - y||^2; solved by the normal equations X^T X w = X^T y.

principal component.def: A unit direction along which a dataset varies the most (computed in the PCA lesson).

trace.def: The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix; it equals the sum of the eigenvalues.

underdetermined system.def: A linear system with fewer independent equations than unknowns; it has infinitely many solutions if it has any.

minimum-norm solution.def: The solution of Ax = b with the smallest norm: A^T (A A^T)^{-1} b for A with independent rows.

row space.def: The span of the rows of A, the column space of A^T. It is orthogonal to the null space.

pseudo-inverse.def: A^+ (np.linalg.pinv): A^+ b is the minimum-norm least-squares solution of Ax = b.

eigenvector.def: A non-zero v with A v = lambda v: a direction the matrix only stretches.

eigenvalue.def: The stretch factor lambda in A v = lambda v; the roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0.

characteristic polynomial.def: det(A - lambda I), a polynomial in lambda whose roots are the eigenvalues.

diagonalization.def: Writing A = V Lambda V^{-1} with eigenvectors in V and eigenvalues in Lambda; then A^k = V Lambda^k V^{-1}.

symmetric matrix.def: A square matrix equal to its transpose.

orthogonal matrix.def: A square matrix Q with Q^T Q = I (orthonormal columns); a rotation or reflection.

spectral theorem.def: Every real symmetric matrix is Q Lambda Q^T with Q orthogonal and Lambda real diagonal.

quadratic form.def: x^T A x for a symmetric matrix A, a sum of terms A_ij x_i x_j.

positive definite.def: x^T A x > 0 for every non-zero x; for symmetric A, all eigenvalues are positive.

positive semidefinite.def: x^T A x >= 0 for every x; for symmetric A, all eigenvalues are at least 0. X^T X always is.

singular value decomposition.def: SVD: A = U Sigma V^T with U, V orthogonal and Sigma diagonal with sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= ... >= 0.

singular value.def: A diagonal entry sigma_i of Sigma in the SVD; sigma_i^2 are the eigenvalues of A^T A.

singular vectors.def: The columns of U (left) and V (right) in the SVD; A v_i = sigma_i u_i.

frobenius norm.def: ||A||_F = square root of the sum of all squared entries; ||A||_F^2 = sum of sigma_i^2.

low-rank approximation.def: A matrix of rank at most k close to A; the best one keeps the k largest SVD terms.

eckart-young theorem.def: The truncated SVD A_k is the best rank-k approximation, with ||A - A_k||_F^2 = sum of the dropped sigma_i^2.

rank-one matrix.def: A non-zero outer product u v^T; every column is a multiple of u.

power iteration.def: A method for the eigenvector whose eigenvalue has the largest absolute value: repeat x <- Ax / ||Ax||. The error shrinks like |lambda_2 / lambda_1|^k.

rayleigh quotient.def: For a unit vector x, the number x^T A x. When x is an eigenvector it equals the eigenvalue, sign included.

deflation.def: Removing a found eigenpair from a symmetric matrix, A - lambda v v^T, so that power iteration finds the next one.

activation function.def: The fixed nonlinear function a neural network applies to every entry after a linear step, such as ReLU, sigmoid or tanh.

tanh.def: The hyperbolic tangent (e^z - e^(-z)) / (e^z + e^(-z)), with values in (-1, 1) and derivative 1 - tanh^2(z).

softplus.def: The function ln(1 + e^z), a smooth version of ReLU whose derivative is the sigmoid.

saturation.def: The flat region of an activation such as sigmoid or tanh for large |z|, where the derivative is near 0 and little gradient passes through.

central difference.def: The derivative estimate (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2h); its error shrinks like h^2. Use h around 1e-5.

gradient check.def: Comparing a hand-derived derivative or gradient with a numerical estimate such as the central difference, to catch mistakes.

partial derivative.def: The derivative of a function of several inputs with respect to one of them, holding all the others fixed.

gradient.def: The vector of all partial derivatives of a scalar function. It points in the direction of steepest increase and has the shape of the input.

directional derivative.def: The rate of change of f along a unit vector u, equal to the dot product of the gradient with u.

level curve.def: A contour line: the set of points where a function takes one fixed value. The gradient is perpendicular to it.

computational graph.def: A diagram of a calculation with one box per intermediate value and arrows showing which values feed which.

forward pass.def: Computing a model's outputs and loss from its inputs, left to right through the computational graph.

local derivative.def: The derivative of one box of a computational graph with respect to one of its direct inputs.

backpropagation.def: Computing the gradient of the loss with the chain rule, from the output back to the parameters, multiplying local derivatives along paths and adding over paths.

upstream gradient.def: During backpropagation, the derivative of the loss with respect to a box's output, which the box multiplies by its local derivative.

autograd.def: PyTorch's automatic differentiation: it records operations on tensors with requires_grad=True and computes gradients when backward() is called.

neuron.def: The smallest unit of a neural network: a linear step w . x + b followed by an activation function.

tensor.def: PyTorch's array type, like a NumPy array but able to record operations for autograd; torch.tensor(0.5) is a one-number tensor.

optimizer.def: The PyTorch object (such as torch.optim.SGD) that updates a model's parameters from their gradients; zero_grad() clears the stored gradients.

jacobian.def: For a function from R^n to R^m, the m x n matrix of first partial derivatives, entry (i, j) = d g_i / d x_j.

hessian.def: The square, symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function; the multivariable version of f''.

convex function.def: A function whose chord between any two points lies on or above its graph; for smooth functions, one whose Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere. Every local minimum is global.

strictly convex.def: Convex with strict inequality for distinct points; it has at most one minimizer. A positive definite Hessian everywhere is enough.

concave.def: A function f is concave when -f is convex: chords lie on or below the graph.

local minimum.def: A point whose value is less than or equal to the values at all nearby points.

global minimum.def: A point whose value is less than or equal to the value everywhere.

critical point.def: A point where the gradient is zero: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point.

saddle point.def: A critical point that is a minimum along some directions and a maximum along others, such as the origin for x^2 - y^2.

logistic regression.def: A classifier for labels 0/1 that predicts p = sigmoid(x . beta) and is trained by minimizing the binary cross-entropy, a convex loss.

gradient descent.def: Minimizing a loss by repeating w <- w - lr * gradient: step against the gradient, which points uphill.

full-batch gradient descent.def: Gradient descent that uses every training example to compute each gradient.

mini-batch.def: A random subset of the training examples (for example 32) used to estimate the gradient for one update.

stochastic gradient descent.def: SGD: gradient descent using gradients from random mini-batches (or single examples) instead of the whole training set.

epoch.def: One pass through the whole training set; with n examples and batch size B it has ceil(n / B) updates.

newton's method.def: The update w <- w - H^(-1) * gradient, which jumps to the minimum of the second-order Taylor model. One step solves a quadratic exactly.

quadratic convergence.def: Error that is roughly squared each step, so the number of correct digits about doubles; Newton's method near a minimum.

damped newton.def: Newton's method with the step multiplied by a learning rate below 1, for stability far from the minimum.

constraint.def: A condition the solution of an optimization problem must satisfy, such as g(x) = 0 or g(x) <= 0.

lagrange multiplier.def: The number lambda in grad f = lambda * grad g at a constrained optimum; one per constraint.

lagrangian.def: The function f(x) - lambda * g(x); its critical points give the candidates for a constrained optimum.

kkt conditions.def: The optimality conditions for inequality constraints: the gradient condition, multipliers >= 0, and a multiplier can be nonzero only for an active constraint.

active constraint.def: An inequality constraint that holds with equality at the solution.

support vector machine.def: SVM: a linear classifier sign(w . x + b) chosen to maximize the margin, by minimizing ||w||^2 / 2 subject to y_i (w . x_i + b) >= 1.

margin.def: For a linear classifier, the distance from the decision boundary to the nearest training points; 1 / ||w|| in the SVM scaling.

support vectors.def: The training points exactly on an SVM's margin; only they have nonzero multipliers and determine w.

soft target.def: A training target that is a probability vector (or a probability between 0 and 1) rather than a one-hot label.

condition number.def: For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the ratio of its largest to smallest eigenvalue. Gradient descent on a quadratic shrinks the error by about (k - 1)/(k + 1) per step at best.

random experiment.def: Anything with an uncertain result, such as rolling a die or drawing a training example at random.

outcome.def: One possible result of a random experiment.

sample space.def: The set of all possible outcomes, written Omega. Two dice have 36 ordered outcomes.

event.def: A set of outcomes (a subset of the sample space); it happens if the outcome lies in it.

probability.def: A function P on events with P(A) >= 0, P(sample space) = 1, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for disjoint A, B.

complement.def: The event 'not A', all outcomes outside A; P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

intersection.def: The event 'A and B': outcomes in both.

union.def: The event 'A or B': outcomes in at least one of them.

inclusion-exclusion.def: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B): the overlap is counted twice, so subtract it once.

mutually exclusive.def: Events that share no outcomes (also called disjoint); P(A and B) = 0.

factorial.def: n! = n (n - 1) ... 1, the number of orderings of n items; 0! = 1.

binomial coefficient.def: C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n - k)!), read 'n choose k': the number of ways to choose k items out of n, ignoring order.

independent events.def: Events with P(A and B) = P(A) P(B); knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other.

conditional probability.def: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B): the probability of A once you know B happened.

prior.def: The probability of a hypothesis before seeing the evidence, such as a base rate P(D).

posterior.def: The probability of a hypothesis after seeing the evidence, P(H | E), computed with Bayes' rule.

likelihood.def: P(evidence | hypothesis); for a model, the probability of the observed data as a function of the parameters (maximized by maximum likelihood).

partition.def: Events that are disjoint and together cover the sample space, so every outcome is in exactly one.

law of total probability.def: P(A) = sum over a partition B_j of P(A | B_j) P(B_j).

bayes' rule.def: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E): posterior = likelihood times prior, divided by the probability of the evidence.

random variable.def: A number determined by the outcome of a random experiment (formally, a function from outcomes to numbers).

discrete random variable.def: A random variable whose possible values can be listed, such as a count or a class label.

continuous random variable.def: A random variable taking values in an interval, described by a density; each single value has probability 0.

distribution.def: The complete description of a random variable's probabilities, given by its PMF, PDF or CDF.

pmf.def: Probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x) of a discrete random variable; its values sum to 1.

cdf.def: Cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x); P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a).

pdf.def: Probability density function f of a continuous random variable: probabilities are areas under f. f can exceed 1.

joint pmf.def: p(x, y) = P(X = x and Y = y) for two discrete random variables.

marginal distribution.def: The distribution of one variable alone, found by summing (or integrating) the joint distribution over the other.

uniform distribution.def: Equal probability (or constant density) over a set; U(a, b) has density 1 / (b - a), mean (a + b) / 2, variance (b - a)^2 / 12.

expectation.def: E[X] = sum of x p(x) (or the integral of x f(x)): the probability-weighted average value. A fair die has E[X] = 3.5.

linearity of expectation.def: E[aX + bY + c] = a E[X] + b E[Y] + c for any random variables, independent or not.

indicator.def: The random variable that is 1 if an event happens and 0 otherwise; its expectation is the event's probability.

covariance.def: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - mean X)(Y - mean Y)] = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y]; positive when X and Y tend to move together.

correlation.def: Cov(X, Y) / (sd X sd Y), between -1 and 1; plus or minus 1 exactly for a linear relation.

covariance matrix.def: For a random vector, the matrix of all covariances Cov(X_i, X_j); symmetric, variances on the diagonal, always positive semidefinite.

bernoulli distribution.def: A 0/1 variable equal to 1 with probability p; mean p, variance p (1 - p).

binomial distribution.def: Bin(n, p): the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials; P(k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k), mean np, variance np(1 - p).

categorical distribution.def: One of k classes with probabilities pi_1, ..., pi_k; a softmax output is one.

standard normal.def: N(0, 1), the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1, usually written Z.

68-95-99.7 rule.def: A normal value lies within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean with probability about 0.683, 0.954 and 0.997.

multivariate normal.def: N(mu, Sigma) for random vectors: density contours are ellipses along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix Sigma.

population.def: The distribution that generates the data; its mean and variance are fixed but unknown.

statistic.def: A number computed from a sample, such as the sample mean.

estimator.def: A statistic used to estimate a population quantity, such as the sample mean for the population mean.

unbiased estimator.def: An estimator whose expectation equals the true value; the n - 1 sample variance is unbiased, the divide-by-n one is not.

correlation matrix.def: The matrix of correlations between features, C_jk / (s_j s_k), with ones on the diagonal; np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False).

median.def: The middle value of sorted data (the mean of the two middle values for even n); barely moved by outliers.

percentile.def: The q-th percentile is the value below which q% of the data lie; np.percentile interpolates linearly between sorted values.

interquartile range.def: IQR = Q3 - Q1, the spread of the middle half of the data; values beyond Q3 + 1.5 IQR or below Q1 - 1.5 IQR are often called outliers.

parametric model.def: A family of distributions p(x; theta) indexed by a parameter theta, such as Bernoulli(p) or N(mu, sigma^2).

iid.def: Independent and identically distributed: independent draws from the same distribution.

maximum likelihood estimate.def: MLE: the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood of the observed data, e.g. k / n for a Bernoulli.

log-likelihood.def: The log of the likelihood, a sum of log-probabilities over examples; same maximizer, no underflow.

negative log-likelihood.def: NLL, minus the log-likelihood, used as a loss; Gaussian noise gives squared error, Bernoulli labels give cross-entropy.

map.def: Maximum a posteriori estimate: maximize likelihood times prior; a Gaussian prior on the weights gives an L2 penalty.

information content.def: The surprise -log p of an outcome with probability p; in bits for log base 2, nats for natural log.

bit.def: The unit of information for base-2 logs; 1 bit = ln 2 = 0.693 nats.

nat.def: The unit of information for natural logs, used by ML losses.

entropy.def: H(p) = -sum p_j log p_j, the expected surprise of a distribution; 0 when one outcome is certain, log k for uniform over k.

binary entropy.def: The entropy of a coin with P(heads) = p: -p log p - (1 - p) log(1 - p).

cross-entropy.def: H(p, q) = -sum p_j log q_j: expected surprise under p when using probabilities q; minimized over q at q = p.

kl divergence.def: D_KL(p || q) = sum p_j log(p_j / q_j) = H(p, q) - H(p); never negative, zero only for q = p, not symmetric.

standard error.def: The standard deviation of an estimate: sigma / sqrt(n) for a mean, sqrt(p (1 - p) / n) for a proportion.

law of large numbers.def: The sample mean of iid draws approaches the true mean as n grows.

central limit theorem.def: For large n, the mean of n iid draws is approximately normal, N(mu, sigma^2 / n), whatever the original distribution.

confidence interval.def: A range such as estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, which contains the true value for about 95% of samples.

monte carlo estimation.def: Estimating a probability or expectation by averaging over many random samples; the error shrinks like 1 / sqrt(n).

bootstrap.def: Estimating a statistic's standard error by recomputing it on many resamples of size n drawn with replacement from the data.

he initialization.def: Drawing a layer's weights with variance 2/C (C inputs) when its inputs come out of a ReLU, so the output variance matches the input variance.

machine learning.def: Writing a program whose behavior is set by fitting numbers to data instead of hand-written rules.

example.def: One data point, one row of a dataset (also called a sample). It has features and, in supervised learning, a label.

feature vector.def: The features of one example written as a list of numbers, such as x = (80, 3).

model.def: A function from feature vectors to predictions with adjustable numbers (parameters) inside it.

parameter.def: A number inside a model that training chooses, such as a weight or the bias.

weight.def: A parameter that multiplies a feature, such as w in w * size + b.

bias term.def: The constant parameter b added to a model's output, such as b in w * size + b.

loss function.def: A function that turns predictions and labels into one number measuring how wrong the model is; training makes it small.

training.def: Running an algorithm that chooses a model's parameters to make the loss on the training examples small (also called fitting).

inference.def: Using a trained model to make predictions on new feature vectors (also called prediction).

hyperparameter.def: A setting chosen before training that training does not change, such as the polynomial degree, k in kNN, or the learning rate.

learning rate.def: A hyperparameter that sets the size of each training update step.

supervised learning.def: Learning from examples that come with labels, to predict the label from the features.

classification.def: A supervised task whose label is one of a fixed set of categories (classes).

unsupervised learning.def: Learning from examples with no labels, to find structure such as clusters.

clustering.def: Grouping similar examples together without labels.

dimensionality reduction.def: Representing data with fewer features while keeping its main structure (PCA, UMAP).

self-supervised learning.def: Learning from unlabeled data by creating targets from the data itself, such as predicting the next word.

reinforcement learning.def: An agent learns which actions to take in an environment from numerical rewards, with no correct answer given per step.

generalization.def: How well a model performs on new examples it was not trained on.

validation set.def: Held-out examples used to compare models and choose hyperparameters (also called the dev set).

model selection.def: Choosing among models or hyperparameter settings, using validation data or cross-validation.

data leakage.def: Information that will not be available at prediction time getting into training or features, which makes evaluation scores too optimistic.

group split.def: A split that keeps all examples from one group (one patient, one user) on the same side.

capacity.def: How flexible a model family is: how many different shapes of function it can fit.

underfitting.def: The model is too simple for the pattern: training and validation error are both high.

overfitting.def: The model fits noise in its training data: training error is low and validation error much higher.

bias (of a model).def: Error from a model being too simple: how far its average prediction, over many possible training sets, is from the truth.

variance (of a model).def: Error from a model reacting to its particular training set: how much its predictions change from one training set to another.

bias-variance trade-off.def: As capacity grows, bias falls and variance rises; the best model balances the two.

learning curve.def: A plot of training and validation error against training set size (or training time).

regularization.def: Any change to training that stops a model from fitting its training data too closely, most often a penalty on the weights.

regularization strength.def: The hyperparameter lambda that multiplies the penalty; larger lambda means a simpler model.

l2 penalty.def: The sum of squared weights added to the loss; shrinks every weight but rarely makes one exactly zero.

ridge regression.def: Linear regression with an L2 penalty on the weights.

weight decay.def: The name for L2 regularization in neural network training.

l1 penalty.def: The sum of absolute values of the weights added to the loss; sets small weights to exactly zero.

lasso.def: Linear regression with an L1 penalty on the weights.

soft thresholding.def: The L1 solution w = sign(a) max(|a| - lambda, 0): move a toward zero by lambda and stop at zero.

sparse.def: Having many entries exactly equal to zero.

elastic net.def: Linear regression with both an L1 and an L2 penalty.

early stopping.def: Keeping the parameters from the training step with the lowest validation loss instead of training to the end.

positive class.def: In binary classification, the class being detected (label 1), such as spam or fraud.

confusion matrix.def: The table of counts of each (actual class, predicted class) pair; in scikit-learn rows are actual and columns predicted.

true positive.def: TP: an actual positive predicted positive.

false positive.def: FP: an actual negative predicted positive (a false alarm).

false negative.def: FN: an actual positive predicted negative (a miss).

true negative.def: TN: an actual negative predicted negative.

precision.def: Of the examples predicted positive, the fraction that are actually positive: TP / (TP + FP).

recall.def: Of the actual positives, the fraction predicted positive: TP / (TP + FN). Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.

f1 score.def: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R) = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN).

specificity.def: The recall of the negative class: TN / (TN + FP).

class imbalance.def: One class being much rarer than another, which makes accuracy misleading.

one-vs-rest.def: Treating one class as positive and all other classes as negative, to get per-class metrics.

macro average.def: The plain mean of a per-class metric over the classes; every class counts equally.

micro average.def: A metric computed once from TP, FP and FN summed over all classes; for single-label problems micro-F1 equals accuracy.

weighted average.def: The mean of a per-class metric weighted by each class's support.

support.def: The number of examples whose true label is a given class.

score.def: A classifier's number for an example, higher meaning more likely positive (often an estimated probability).

threshold.def: The cutoff t: an example is predicted positive when its score is at least t.

true positive rate.def: TPR = TP / (TP + FN), the same as recall.

false positive rate.def: FPR = FP / (FP + TN), the fraction of actual negatives predicted positive.

roc curve.def: The plot of true positive rate against false positive rate over all thresholds.

auc.def: Area under the ROC curve: the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs in which the positive has the higher score, ties counting one half.

precision-recall curve.def: The plot of precision against recall over all thresholds; more informative than ROC when positives are rare.

average precision.def: A one-number summary of the precision-recall curve, roughly the area under it.

rmse.def: Root mean squared error, the square root of the MSE; in the label's units.

mae.def: Mean absolute error: the average of |y - y_hat|.

r squared.def: R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, negative is worse.

cross-validation.def: Estimating performance by training and validating several times on different splits of the training data.

k-fold cross-validation.def: Cut the data into k folds; train on k - 1 folds and validate on the remaining one, k times; average the scores.

fold.def: One of the k equal parts of the data in k-fold cross-validation.

leave-one-out.def: k-fold cross-validation with k = n: each fold is a single example.

stratified k-fold.def: k-fold cross-validation in which every fold keeps the class proportions of the whole set.

time-series split.def: Validation that always trains on earlier data and validates on later data.

grid search.def: Trying every combination of listed hyperparameter values.

random search.def: Trying a fixed number of randomly sampled hyperparameter combinations.

nested cross-validation.def: An outer cross-validation loop that scores the whole tuning procedure, with an inner cross-validation inside each outer fold for tuning.

preprocessing.def: Turning raw data into a clean numeric feature matrix: imputing, encoding, scaling.

standardization.def: Rescaling a feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: z = (x - mean) / std, with statistics from the training set.

min-max scaling.def: Rescaling a feature to [0, 1] with (x - min) / (max - min).

pipeline.def: A chain of preprocessing steps and a model that is fit and applied as one unit, so transforms are fit on training data only.

categorical feature.def: A feature whose values are names from a fixed set, such as a city.

ordinal encoding.def: Coding ordered categories as 0, 1, 2, ...; reasonable only when the order and spacing are real.

imputation.def: Filling missing values with estimates, such as the training median of the column.

missing indicator.def: A 0/1 feature that records whether a value was missing before imputation.

feature engineering.def: Building new features from existing ones, such as ratios, date parts, logs or bins.

binning.def: Turning a numeric feature into ranges (bins), such as Small, Medium, Large.

linear regression.def: A model that predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features plus a constant: y_hat = w . x + b.

intercept.def: The constant b in a linear model, the prediction when every feature is 0; another name for the bias term.

design matrix.def: The (n, d) matrix X whose row i is the feature vector of example i.

closed-form solution.def: A formula that gives the answer directly, with no iterating, such as w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y.

sample weight.def: A number s_i >= 0 saying how much example i counts in a weighted loss; weight 2 acts like two copies, weight 0 removes it.

centered data.def: Data with each column's mean subtracted, so every column has mean 0: X_c = X - X.mean(axis=0).

odds.def: p / (1 - p) for an event of probability p; odds of 3 mean 3 to 1, p = 0.75.

log-odds.def: ln(p / (1 - p)), the inverse of the sigmoid; logistic regression models the log-odds as w . x + b.

decision boundary.def: The set of inputs where a classifier is exactly undecided; for logistic regression the hyperplane w . x + b = 0.

linear classifier.def: A classifier whose decision boundary is a hyperplane w . x + b = 0, such as logistic regression or the perceptron.

log-loss.def: Binary cross-entropy: -[y ln p + (1 - y) ln(1 - p)], minus the log of the probability given to the true label.

softmax regression.def: Logistic regression for K classes: logits Z = XW + b, probabilities softmax(Z) row by row, trained with cross-entropy; gradient X^T (P - Y) / n.

perceptron.def: A linear classifier with labels -1/+1 trained by the rule: on a mistake y(w . x + b) <= 0, add y x to w and y to b.

linearly separable.def: A labeled dataset that some hyperplane splits with every +1 example strictly on one side and every -1 example strictly on the other.

xor.def: Exclusive or: (0,0), (1,1) in one class and (0,1), (1,0) in the other; the standard example of data no line can separate.

proximal gradient descent.def: For a loss = smooth part + L1 penalty: take a gradient step on the smooth part, then soft-threshold by (learning rate x lambda). Also called ISTA; it trains lasso with exact zeros.

lazy learner.def: A model whose training step only stores the data and does all the work at prediction time, such as kNN.

majority vote.def: Predicting the label that appears most often among a set of votes (neighbors in kNN, trees in a forest).

feature selection.def: Choosing a subset of the features to use and dropping the rest, usually the ones that carry little information about the label.

manhattan distance.def: The L1 distance sum_j |a_j - b_j|, the length of a path along grid lines.

curse of dimensionality.def: Problems that appear in many dimensions; for kNN, distances to the nearest and farthest points become nearly equal, so nearness says less.

decision tree.def: A model that predicts by asking a sequence of questions 'is feature j at most t?' from the root down to a leaf, which stores the prediction.

node (tree).def: One box of a decision tree: an internal node asks a question; a leaf stores a prediction.

root (tree).def: The first node of a decision tree, which every example passes through.

leaf.def: A node of a tree with no question; it predicts the majority class (or mean label) of the training examples that reach it.

split.def: A node's question 'x_j <= t?' that sends each example to the left or right child.

depth (tree).def: The number of questions on the longest root-to-leaf path of a tree.

impurity.def: A score of how mixed the classes in a tree node are: 0 for a single class, largest for an even mix (Gini or entropy).

gini impurity.def: 1 - sum_c p_c^2 for class fractions p_c: the chance two random draws from the node have different classes. 0 when pure, 0.5 at a 50/50 split of two classes.

weighted impurity.def: The impurity of a split's children, each weighted by its share of the examples: (n_L/n) I(left) + (n_R/n) I(right).

information gain.def: Parent entropy minus the weighted entropy of the children; how much a split reduces uncertainty about the label.

greedy algorithm.def: An algorithm that makes the best choice at each step without looking ahead, such as choosing tree splits one node at a time.

pruning.def: Removing branches from a grown decision tree to reduce overfitting.

ensemble.def: A model made of many models whose predictions are combined by a vote or an average.

bootstrap sample.def: n examples drawn with replacement from a dataset of size n; it contains about 63.2% of the distinct examples.

bagging.def: Bootstrap aggregating: train one model per bootstrap sample and combine them by vote or average; reduces variance.

out-of-bag.def: The training examples left out of a model's bootstrap sample (about 36.8%); predicting each example with the models that never saw it gives the OOB score.

random forest.def: Bagged decision trees in which every split chooses among a random subset of the features, which makes the trees less correlated.

boosting.def: Building an ensemble in sequence, each new small model trained to fix the errors of the ensemble so far; reduces bias.

decision stump.def: A decision tree of depth 1: one question and two leaves.

gradient boosting.def: Boosting in which each new tree is fit to the negative gradient of the loss (the residuals, for squared error) and added with a small learning rate.

soft-margin svm.def: An SVM that allows margin violations, each costing C times its slack: minimize ||w||^2 / 2 + C sum of hinge losses.

slack.def: xi_i >= 0, how far example i falls short of the margin condition y_i f(x_i) >= 1 in a soft-margin SVM.

hinge loss.def: max(0, 1 - y f(x)) for labels y in {-1, +1}: zero outside the margin, growing linearly inside it and on the wrong side.

kernel (svm).def: A function K(x, z) equal to the dot product phi(x) . phi(z) of mapped features, computed without forming phi.

kernel trick.def: Replacing every dot product in an algorithm (such as the SVM) with a kernel, to get a nonlinear model at the cost of a linear one.

polynomial kernel.def: K(x, z) = (x . z + c)^p, the dot product of all monomial features up to degree p.

rbf kernel.def: Radial basis function (Gaussian) kernel exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2): 1 for identical points, near 0 for distant ones; larger gamma means narrower bumps.

centroid.def: The center of a cluster; in k-means, the mean of the points assigned to it.

inertia.def: The k-means objective: the sum over all points of the squared distance to their own cluster center (within-cluster sum of squares).

k-means++.def: An initialization for k-means: the first center uniformly at random, each next one drawn with probability proportional to the squared distance to the nearest chosen center.

elbow method.def: Choosing k by plotting inertia against k and picking the bend after which more clusters reduce inertia little.

silhouette score.def: The mean over points of (b - a) / max(a, b), with a the mean distance to the own cluster and b to the nearest other cluster; from -1 to 1, higher is better.

hierarchical clustering.def: Clustering that builds a tree of nested clusterings; cutting the tree at a height gives one clustering.

agglomerative clustering.def: Bottom-up hierarchical clustering: start with one cluster per point and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters.

dendrogram.def: The tree diagram of a hierarchical clustering; two branches join at the height (distance) where their clusters merged.

linkage.def: The rule for the distance between two clusters: single (closest pair), complete (farthest pair), average, or Ward (increase in inertia).

dbscan.def: Density-based clustering: core points have at least min_samples points within eps; clusters grow through core points; other far points are noise (-1).

core point.def: In DBSCAN, a point with at least min_samples points (itself included) within distance eps.

border point.def: In DBSCAN, a point that is not core but lies within eps of a core point; it joins that cluster.

noise point.def: In DBSCAN, a point that is neither core nor border; labeled -1.

spectral clustering.def: Clustering by building a similarity graph, embedding points with the eigenvectors of its Laplacian for the smallest eigenvalues, then running k-means.

graph laplacian.def: L = D - W for a similarity matrix W and the diagonal matrix D of its row sums; v^T L v = (1/2) sum W_ij (v_i - v_j)^2.

pca.def: Principal component analysis: project centered data onto the top-k eigenvectors of its covariance matrix (equivalently, the top right singular vectors of X_c).

scores (pca).def: The coordinates of the data along the principal components, Z = X_c W_k, shape (n, k).

reconstruction (pca).def: Mapping scores back to the original space, Z W_k^T + mean: the projection of each point onto the kept subspace.

explained variance ratio.def: lambda_j / sum of all eigenvalues: the fraction of the total variance carried by principal component j.

scree plot.def: A plot of the covariance eigenvalues (or explained variance ratios) in decreasing order, used to choose how many components to keep.

embedding.def: A representation of each data point as a vector in a new space, such as the 2D coordinates a t-SNE or UMAP map assigns.

t-sne.def: t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding: a nonlinear 2D map that matches neighbor probabilities by minimizing KL divergence; keeps neighborhoods, distorts gaps and cluster sizes.

perplexity.def: t-SNE's setting for the effective number of neighbors each point's Gaussian bump covers (typically 5 to 50).

umap.def: Uniform manifold approximation and projection: a nonlinear map that lays out a nearest-neighbor graph in 2D; favors local neighborhoods over global distances.

estimator (scikit-learn).def: Any scikit-learn object that learns from data with fit; hyperparameters go in its constructor and learned values end in an underscore.

dataframe.def: A pandas table: rows, and named columns that each hold one dtype. Built with pd.DataFrame({name: list, ...}) or pd.read_csv.

series.def: One pandas column: a sequence of values plus an index label for each value. df["amount"] is a Series.

index (pandas).def: The row labels of a Series or DataFrame, shown at the left of a printout. By default 0, 1, 2, ...; filtering keeps the original labels.

object dtype.def: The dtype pandas gives a column of Python strings (or mixed Python objects). It prints as object, not str.

summary statistics.def: A few numbers that describe a column: count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles, maximum. df.describe() prints them.

chained assignment.def: Assigning through two sets of brackets, as in df[mask]["col"] = v. The first brackets make a temporary table, so the original is not changed; use df.loc[mask, "col"] = v.

str accessor.def: The .str attribute of a Series of strings. s.str.strip(), s.str.lower() and so on run a string method on every value and return a new Series.

whitespace.def: Spaces, tabs and newlines. strip() removes it from both ends of a string, never from the middle.

title case.def: Capital first letter on every word, the rest lowercase: str.title() turns "united kingdom" into "United Kingdom" (and "usa" into "Usa").

regular expression.def: A pattern language for text in which some characters are special; the dot matches any character. str.contains uses one unless you pass regex=False.

missing value.def: An entry with no data. pandas shows it as NaN (or None in object columns) and isna() finds it; a file loaded with keep_default_na=False shows it as the empty string instead.

parse.def: To read text and turn it into a value of another type, such as the string "2.5" into the float 2.5.

lexicographic order.def: Dictionary order for strings: compare character by character using character codes. Digit strings do not sort like numbers ("10" < "9"), and uppercase letters come before lowercase.

rank (ordering).def: The position of a value in sorted order, starting at 1. With ties, the method decides: "min" gives ties the smallest position (1, 1, 3), "dense" (1, 1, 2), "average" (1.5, 1.5, 3).

split-apply-combine.def: The groupby pattern: split the rows into groups by a key, apply a computation to each group, combine the results into one table indexed by the key.

named aggregation.def: The agg form new_column=(source_column, function), as in df.groupby("customer").agg(total=("amount", "sum")); it names each output column.

multiindex.def: A pandas index with several levels, such as (customer, category) after grouping by two columns. reset_index() turns the levels into ordinary columns.

join.def: Combining two tables by matching the values of a key column: each pair of rows with equal keys gives one row of the result. df.merge(other, on=key, how=...).

join key.def: The column whose values are matched in a join, such as product_code. Keys match only if they are equal values of the same type.

left join.def: A join that keeps every row of the left table in its order, with NaN in the right table's columns where no key matches. merge(..., how="left").

inner join.def: A join that keeps only the keys found in both tables; unmatched rows are dropped. The default of merge.

index alignment.def: pandas combines two Series by matching index labels, not positions; a label found in only one of them gives NaN.

categorical dtype.def: A pandas dtype that stores values as a fixed list of categories, as pd.cut returns. Convert with astype(str) before writing exact text.

quantile.def: A value with a given fraction q of the data below it, such as the 0.75 quantile. pandas and NumPy default to linear interpolation between sorted values.

quartile.def: The quantiles at 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75, written Q1, Q2 (the median) and Q3.

linear interpolation.def: For quantiles: with sorted values x_0..x_{n-1} and position h = (n - 1)q, take x_i + f(x_{i+1} - x_i), where i is the integer part of h and f its fraction.

outlier.def: A value far from the bulk of the data. The IQR rule flags values above Q3 + 1.5 IQR or below Q1 - 1.5 IQR.

format code.def: A short string that says how to write a number as text: "%.6f" means fixed-point with six digits after the decimal point, so 2.5 becomes 2.500000.

csv quoting.def: The CSV rule for text containing a comma or a quote: wrap it in double quotes and double any quote inside. to_csv and read_csv handle it for you.

histogram.def: A plot that cuts the range of a variable into equal-width bins and draws a bar for the count in each; it shows the shape of a distribution. plt.hist(x, bins=20).

axes (matplotlib).def: One panel of a matplotlib figure, with its own methods such as ax.hist and ax.set_title. plt.subplots(1, 2) returns a figure and two axes.

rolling window.def: The current row plus a fixed number of rows just before it. s.rolling(3, min_periods=2).mean() averages the present values in each such window and gives NaN when fewer than 2 are present.

reshaping.def: Changing a table between long and wide format without changing its numbers, with pivot_table, unstack, stack or melt.

long format.def: A table layout with one row per observation and one column per variable, such as one row per sale with its store, category and amount. Filtering, grouping and joining work on this shape.

wide format.def: A table layout with one row per entity and one column per value of a second key, such as one row per store and one column per category. pivot_table produces it; melt turns it back into long format.

pivot table.def: A wide table built from long data: the distinct values of one column become the rows, those of another become the columns, and each cell aggregates a value column over the rows with that pair of keys (pandas pivot_table).

device.def: The hardware a tensor or model lives on, such as the CPU or a GPU. In the contest it is always the CPU.

float32.def: 32-bit floating point (about 7 significant digits). PyTorch's default float dtype; NumPy's default is float64.

contiguous.def: A tensor whose entries sit in memory in row-major order. permute and .T give non-contiguous tensors, so view fails on them and reshape copies.

leaf tensor.def: A tensor made directly rather than computed from other tensors. Only leaves that require grad get a .grad; model parameters are leaves.

nn.parameter.def: A tensor wrapped as a learnable number of a module. Assigned to self.name in __init__, it is registered: it appears in parameters(), trains, and is saved in state_dict. requires_grad is True by default.

register (a parameter or module).def: What nn.Module does when you assign an nn.Parameter or a module to self.name: it records it, so parameters(), state_dict() and print(model) include it. Plain tensors and Python lists are not registered.

buffer.def: A tensor stored with self.register_buffer(name, t): part of the model and saved in state_dict, but not a parameter, so it never trains. BatchNorm's running mean is one.

submodule.def: A module stored as an attribute of another module. Its parameters count as the parent's, with dotted names like hidden.weight.

independent (random quantities).def: Random quantities are independent when knowing some of them tells you nothing about the others; then E[XY] = E[X] E[Y], and the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances.

variance-preserving initialization.def: Drawing a linear layer's weights with standard deviation 1/sqrt(in_features), so each output has the same variance as each input (Var y = C sigma_w^2 sigma^2).

multilayer perceptron.def: A neural network made of linear layers with activation functions between them (MLP for short).

nn.sequential.def: A container module that feeds its input through the given layers in order. Its parameters are named by position: 0.weight, 2.bias.

nn.modulelist.def: A list of modules that registers every layer, so their parameters count and train. Use it instead of a Python list when forward needs a loop.

numel.def: Number of elements: t.numel() is the number of entries of a tensor. sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) counts a model's parameters.

convolution layer.def: nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, k): slides out_channels filters of shape (in_channels, k, k) over an image. It has in*out*k*k weights plus out biases; output height floor((H + 2p - k)/s) + 1.

crossentropyloss.def: nn.CrossEntropyLoss(): takes raw logits of shape (N, C) and class indices of shape (N,) with dtype torch.long; applies softmax itself and returns the mean of -log p(true class).

bcewithlogitsloss.def: nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(): binary cross-entropy with the sigmoid built in. Takes logits and float 0/1 targets of the same shape.

reduction (loss argument).def: The loss argument that says how per-entry losses combine: 'mean' (default), 'sum', or 'none' (return them all).

adam.def: An optimizer that scales each parameter's step using running averages of its past gradients; torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=1e-3) is a common default.

full-batch.def: Training where every step uses the whole training set, so one epoch is one step.

training step.def: The four lines repeated in every training loop: optimizer.zero_grad(); loss = loss_fn(model(X), y); loss.backward(); optimizer.step().

tensordataset.def: torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X, y): a dataset whose item i is (X[i], y[i]); the tensors must share their first axis.

dataloader.def: torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch_size, shuffle): yields mini-batches of stacked samples; len(loader) is the number of batches, ceil(N / B) unless drop_last=True.

dataset (pytorch).def: A class with __len__ (number of samples) and __getitem__ (sample i), usually a subclass of torch.utils.data.Dataset; a DataLoader batches it.

dropout.def: nn.Dropout(p): in training mode, sets each entry to 0 with probability p and scales the rest by 1/(1-p); in eval mode it does nothing. It has no parameters.

eval mode.def: model.eval() sets training=False on every submodule, so dropout is off and batch norm uses its stored statistics. It does not stop gradient tracking or freeze parameters.

state_dict.def: model.state_dict(): a dict from dotted names to tensors holding every registered parameter and buffer. torch.save it; load it into a model of the same architecture with load_state_dict.

map_location.def: The torch.load argument that says where to put the loaded tensors; map_location="cpu" loads a checkpoint saved on a GPU onto the CPU.

pretrained model.def: A model whose parameters were already trained, usually on a large dataset such as ImageNet, and are reused for a new task.

transfer learning.def: Reusing a pretrained model's layers for a new task, typically by keeping its backbone and training a new head.

fine-tuning.def: Training some or all of a pretrained model's parameters on a new task, usually with a small learning rate.

backbone.def: The part of a network that turns the input into a feature vector; in transfer learning it is reused (often frozen) and a new head is put on top.

head.def: The last part of a network, usually one nn.Linear, that turns features into the task's outputs (for example class logits). Replaced when the task changes.

freezing.def: Setting requires_grad=False on parameters so training leaves them unchanged: module.requires_grad_(False). A new layer added afterward still trains.

forward hook.def: A function attached with module.register_forward_hook(fn) that PyTorch calls as fn(module, inputs, output) after the module's forward; used to read intermediate shapes. Remove it with the returned handle.

global average pooling.def: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1): averages each channel over all positions, turning (N, C, H, W) into (N, C, 1, 1) for any H and W.

layer.def: A group of neurons that read the same input; a fully connected layer computes phi(W x + b) with one row of W per neuron.

pre-activation.def: The values z = W x + b of a layer before the activation function is applied.

activation (value).def: The output a = phi(z) of a layer after its activation function; the input to the next layer.

fully connected layer.def: A layer in which every output depends on every input through its own weight: nn.Linear in PyTorch.

neural network.def: A model made of layers, each feeding the next; with activation functions between the layers it can compute nonlinear functions.

input layer.def: The data fed to a network, counted as layer 0; it has no weights.

hidden layer.def: A layer between the input and the output; the data never says what its values should be.

output layer.def: The last layer of a network; it usually has no activation and outputs real numbers or logits.

width (of a layer).def: The number of units (neurons) in a layer.

depth (of a network).def: The number of layers with weights in a network.

affine function.def: A linear function plus a constant, x -> W x + b. Composing affine functions gives another affine function.

piecewise linear function.def: A function that is affine on each of finitely many regions; every ReLU network computes one.

kink.def: A point where a piecewise linear function changes slope; ReLU(x - t) has one at x = t.

universal approximation theorem.def: A network with one hidden layer and a non-polynomial activation (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region, given enough hidden units. It does not say how many, or whether training finds them.

threshold function.def: Theta(z) = 1 if z >= 0 and 0 if z < 0 (the step or Heaviside function); the 2026 paper used Theta(0) = 1.

threshold unit.def: A neuron Theta(w . x + b) that outputs 1 on one closed side of the hyperplane w . x + b = 0 and 0 on the other.

half-plane.def: The set of points on one side of a line, such as {(x, y) : a x + b y + c >= 0}.

convex polygon.def: A polygon that contains the whole segment between any two of its points; it is the intersection (AND) of the half-planes of its edges.

1d convolution.def: A layer that applies the same small set of weights at every position of a sequence: nn.Conv1d(1, 1, 3, padding=1) gives y_i = w0 x_(i-1) + w1 x_i + w2 x_(i+1) + bias.

leakyrelu.def: z for z > 0 and alpha z otherwise (default alpha = 0.01): a ReLU whose gradient is never exactly 0.

gelu.def: Gaussian error linear unit, z Phi(z) with Phi the standard normal CDF: a smooth ReLU that dips to about -0.17 near z = -0.75. Used in transformers.

vanishing gradient problem.def: In a deep network the gradient is a product of one factor per layer; if the factors are below 1 (sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25), the early layers get almost no gradient and barely train.

exploding gradient problem.def: The opposite of vanishing gradients: per-layer factors above 1 multiply into huge gradients and unstable updates. Gradient clipping is the usual fix.

dead relu.def: A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input, so it outputs 0, gets zero gradient, and never recovers.

outlier (in a loss).def: A target far from the rest. Under MSE its gradient grows with its error and can dominate training; under MAE or Huber it counts like any other mistake.

huber loss.def: 0.5 e^2 for |e| <= delta and delta (|e| - 0.5 delta) beyond: quadratic for small errors, linear for large ones. nn.HuberLoss(delta=1.0).

binary cross-entropy.def: -[t ln q + (1 - t) ln(1 - q)] with q = sigmoid(z); its gradient with respect to the logit z is q - t. nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss takes z.

label smoothing.def: Training on t = (1 - eps) y + eps / K instead of the one-hot y, so the best logits stay finite and the model is less overconfident. nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=eps).

knowledge distillation.def: Training a small student network on the soft probability outputs of a larger trained teacher network.

symmetry (initialization).def: If all units of a layer start with the same weights they get the same gradients and stay identical forever; random initialization breaks the symmetry.

fan-in.def: The number of inputs each output of a layer sums over: in_features for nn.Linear, in_channels * k * k for a convolution.

fan-out.def: The number of outputs of a layer that each input feeds: out_features for nn.Linear.

lecun initialization.def: Weights with variance 1 / fan-in, so a layer keeps the variance of its inputs (the 2026 P7.2 answer sigma_w = 1/sqrt(C)).

xavier initialization.def: Glorot initialization: weights with variance 2 / (fan-in + fan-out), a compromise between the forward and backward passes; for tanh and sigmoid. Uniform bound sqrt(6 / (fan-in + fan-out)).

momentum.def: An optimizer that steps along a running velocity v <- mu v + g (theta <- theta - lr v); steady gradient directions speed up by up to 1/(1 - mu), zigzags cancel. SGD(momentum=0.9).

rmsprop.def: An optimizer that divides each gradient by the square root of a running average of its squares, so every parameter moves about lr per step.

bias correction.def: In Adam, dividing the running averages m and v by 1 - beta^t, because they start at 0 and are too small for the first steps.

adamw.def: Adam with decoupled weight decay: shrink the weights by lr * lambda directly, then take the Adam step with the loss gradient alone. torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr, weight_decay=0.01).

learning rate schedule.def: A rule that changes the learning rate during training, such as StepLR (multiply by gamma every few epochs) or CosineAnnealingLR; scheduler.step() once per epoch.

warmup.def: Starting training with a small learning rate and raising it over the first steps or epochs, to avoid large early updates from random weights.

parameter groups.def: A list of dicts passed to an optimizer, each with its own params and options (for example weight_decay=0 for biases).

inverted dropout.def: Dropout that rescales the surviving entries by 1/(1 - p) during training, so the layer is the identity at test time. PyTorch's nn.Dropout works this way.

patience.def: In early stopping, the number of epochs without a new best validation loss to wait before stopping.

data augmentation.def: Creating extra training examples by label-preserving transformations (flips, crops, noise), applied to the training set only.

batch normalization.def: nn.BatchNorm1d/2d: normalize each feature (channel) with the batch's mean and biased variance, then gamma x_hat + beta. Training mode uses batch statistics and updates running averages; eval mode uses the running averages.

running statistics.def: Batch norm's buffers running_mean and running_var: exponential moving averages of batch statistics (momentum 0.1, unbiased variance) used in eval mode.

exponential moving average.def: avg <- (1 - m) avg + m new: a running average in which old values fade out geometrically. Batch norm's running statistics and Adam's m and v are examples.

layer normalization.def: nn.LayerNorm(D): normalize each example over its last D features with its own mean and variance, then gamma x_hat + beta. No running statistics; identical in train and eval mode. Used in transformers.

embedding layer.def: nn.Embedding(n, d): a learned table of n vectors of length d; index i returns row i. Equivalent to a bias-free linear layer applied to a one-hot vector. n * d parameters.

embedding dimension.def: The length d of each embedding vector, a hyperparameter.

word embedding.def: A vector per word, trained (as in word2vec or GloVe) so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.

similarity matrix.def: For unit-length rows W, S = W W^T: entry (i, j) is the cosine similarity of items i and j, with 1 on the diagonal.

mean pooling.def: Averaging a sequence's token vectors into one vector, for example emb(idx).mean(dim=1).

loss curve.def: A plot of training (and validation) loss against steps or epochs; its shape shows learning-rate problems, underfitting and overfitting.

gradient clipping.def: Rescaling all gradients together so their total L2 norm is at most max_norm, keeping their direction: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, max_norm), between backward() and step().

overfit one batch.def: A debugging check: train on 10 to 20 examples; a correct model and loop drive the loss near 0, so if it does not, the bug is in the code.

convolutional neural network.def: A network built mainly from convolution layers (CNN for short); the standard model for images.

channel.def: One of the grids that make up an image or feature map tensor: a color image has 3 (red, green, blue); a conv layer's output has out_channels. PyTorch stores images as (N, C, H, W).

kernel (convolution).def: The small grid of weights a convolution slides over its input, also called a filter. In nn.Conv2d each output channel has a kernel of shape (in_channels, k, k).

cross-correlation.def: Sliding a kernel over the input and summing kernel times input at each position, without flipping the kernel. It is what deep learning calls convolution (mathematical convolution flips the kernel first).

feature map.def: The output of one channel of a convolution layer: a grid saying how strongly that kernel's pattern appears at each position.

local connectivity.def: Each output of a convolution depends only on a small window of the input, not on every input value.

weight sharing.def: A convolution uses the same kernel at every position, so its parameter count does not depend on the image size.

translation equivariance.def: Shifting the input shifts the output in the same way: a convolution (stride 1) finds a pattern wherever it is.

padding.def: Zeros added around the input before a convolution or pooling window slides: p rows above and below and p columns on each side, so H becomes H + 2p.

same padding.def: Padding that keeps the output the same size as the input at stride 1: p = (k - 1)/2 for an odd kernel, d(k - 1)/2 with dilation d. padding='same' in PyTorch.

valid convolution.def: A convolution with no padding, so the kernel only visits positions where it fits inside the input: output H - k + 1 at stride 1.

stride.def: How many positions a convolution or pooling window moves at each step. Output size floor((H + 2p - d(k - 1) - 1)/s) + 1.

dilation.def: Spacing between a kernel's taps: with dilation d a k-tap kernel spans d(k - 1) + 1 positions but keeps k weights per axis.

1x1 convolution.def: A convolution with kernel size 1: it mixes channels at each pixel without looking at neighbors (C_in * C_out weights). Also called a pointwise convolution.

grouped convolution.def: A convolution with groups=g: input and output channels are split into g groups and each output group reads only its input group. Weight (C_out, C_in/g, k, k), so g times fewer weights.

depthwise convolution.def: A grouped convolution with groups = in_channels: each channel is filtered by its own k x k kernel and channels never mix.

depthwise separable convolution.def: A depthwise convolution followed by a 1x1 convolution; it does the job of one ordinary convolution with far fewer parameters (MobileNet).

multiply-accumulate.def: One multiplication added to a running sum (MAC). A convolution performs H_out * W_out * C_out * (C_in/g) * k^2 of them.

flops.def: Floating-point operations: multiplications and additions counted separately, so about 2 x the number of multiply-accumulates. Conventions vary; use the one a problem states.

pooling.def: A layer that slides a window over each channel and applies a fixed function (max or mean) instead of learned weights. No parameters; the channel count is unchanged. Default stride = kernel size.

max pooling.def: Pooling that keeps the largest value in each window: nn.MaxPool2d(k). Its gradient goes only to the position of the max in each window.

average pooling.def: Pooling that keeps the mean of each window: nn.AvgPool2d(k). Its gradient is shared equally over the window.

adaptive pooling.def: Pooling that fixes the output size and chooses the windows to fit: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((h, w)) returns (N, C, h, w) for any input size.

gradient routing.def: How max pooling backpropagates: each output's gradient goes to the input that was the max of its window (the first one on ties in PyTorch); other inputs get 0, and overlapping wins add up.

receptive field.def: The patch of input pixels that can affect one unit of a feature map. After layer l: r_l = r_(l-1) + (k_eff - 1) j_(l-1), starting from r_0 = 1.

jump (receptive field).def: The distance in input pixels between neighboring units of a layer's output: the product of all strides so far.

feature hierarchy.def: Early CNN layers (small receptive field, high resolution) detect edges and colors; deeper layers (large receptive field, low resolution, many channels) detect parts and whole objects.

lenet-5.def: An early CNN (1998, digits): two 5x5 convolutions with pooling, then three linear layers; 61,706 parameters on 32x32 inputs.

vgg.def: A 2014 CNN family built from 3x3 convolutions with padding 1 and 2x2 max pools, channels 64 to 512; VGG-16 has 138 million parameters, mostly in its linear head.
